newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban win Pakistan recognition as Dostum flees.
newsitem.headline: Taleban win Pakistan recognition as Dostum flees.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban movement tightened its grip on the north of the country and won vital diplomatic recognition from Pakistan on Sunday as former opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum fled to Turkey.

The Taleban government appealed for world recognition after its sweeping weekend victories secured control over most of Afghanistan. Pakistan, which has always denied furnishing support to the Taleban, responded immediately.

But key western neighbour Iran said it was not yet ready to recognise the Taleban. President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani said his country would wait until the Kabul government was recognised by the United Nations.
Russia and its Central Asian allies, alarmed at the spread of Islamic fundamentalism, expressed concern and tightened border security against a possible flood of refugees.
General Abdul Malik, whose switch of sides on Monday to the Taleban triggered Dostum's collapse, promised a strict Islamic regime in the northern areas under his control, centred on Mazar-i-Sharif.

Following an appeal for worldwide diplomatic recognition by Afghanistan's ambassador to Islamabad, Pakistan became the first country to recognise the Taleban Islamic movement's government, set up last September when the fighters captured Kabul.

"I am happy to announce that the government of Pakistan has now decided to accord formal recognition to the new government of the Islamic State of Afghanistan," Pakistan Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan announced.
He said Pakistan had previously withheld recognition to "give time for the promotion of a broad-based government through peaceful negotiations",
General Abdul Rashid Dostum, ousted from his fiefdom in northern Afghanistan by Islamic Taleban fighters, arrived on Sunday in the Turkish capital Ankara, the Turkish Foreign Ministry said.
Turkey was widely reported to have supported the ethnic Uzbek leader Dostum, along with Uzbekistan. Turks and Uzbeks share common ethnic and linguistic links.
General Abdul Malik, the opposition military leader whose mutiny toppled Dostum this weekend, promised a new Islamic order in the north.
"There will be Islamic Shariah (law) in the north," Malik, an ethnic Uzbek, told a news conference in the main norther city of Mazar-i-Sharif, one day after his troops swept in the northern capital.
"I am a son of Islam, my ancestors were Moslems and I was not educated at Moscow as Dostum was," he said in response to a question about his Islamic credentials.

Malik, who was Dostum's deputy until he staged his revolt last Monday in favour of the Taleban movement, said an Islamic Afghanistan would not threaten Russia or Central Asian republics on its northern frontier.

"We don't want to attack Russia," he said. "We want the Central Asian countries to be independent and separate from the (former) Soviet Union. We want Islam, but it is up to the people in those countries."
The former Soviet republics of Central Asia, alarmed by the rise of Moslem fundamentalism, hastily beefed up their border security on Sunday after the Taleban's advances.
"Uzbekistan's border troops are taking measures to reinforce the (Afghan) border to exclude any provocations," said a statement issued by the foreign ministry in Tashkent.

A representative of the Russian border guards in Tajikistan told Reuters there had been an increased influx of refugees from Afghanistan into Tajikistan through the checkpoint at Nizhny Pyandzh, some 200 km (125 miles) south of the Tajik capital Dushanbe.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov held talks with his security advisers late on Saturday on the Afghan crisis. Security officials also met on Sunday morning to discuss ways of maintaining stability.

Less than two weeks ago the Taleban government protested at being left out of a summit meeting of the 10-nation Economic Cooperation Organisation at Dushanbe, capital of Tajikistan, which was attended by ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani.
Russian border troops have also been put on alert in Kyrgyzstan, Interfax news agency said on Sunday.
In Moscow, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov warned the Taleban not to violate the borders of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), successor to the Sovet Union.

Mazar-i-Sharif, the last major city to hold out against the Taleban, appeared on Sunday to be under the full control of ethnic Uzbek fighters who had until last week been part of an alliance opposing the purist Islamic movement.

Taleban official Mullah Wakhil Ahmed Motawakhil told Reuters in Kabul the towns of Kunduz and Baghlan east of Mazar came under Taleban control when fighters from one faction in the alliance switched sides.

"Former Hezb-i-Islami fighters in Kunduz and Baghlan have joined the Taleban and the towns are now under their control." said Motawakhil, speaking by telephone from the Taleban's headquarters in the city of Kandahar.
The Pakistan-based Afghan news service said the provinces of Kunduz and Baghlan and nearby Samangan province, including its capital Aibak, had fallen to the Taleban on Sunday.

The Taleban advance ends an eight-month deadlock between the purist Islamic movement and a fragile coalition linking Dostum with former government forces of Burhanuddin Rabbani, Gulbuddin Hekmatyar's Hezb-i-Islami and the mainly Shi'ite Hezb-i-Wahdat.
The Taleban sweep has left the alliance in tatters and stranded from supply lines in the Hindu Kush mountains.
A Shi'ite Moslem militia was still offering resistance in the central city of Bamiyan, while former government military commander Ahmed Shah Masood holds part of the north east.
